item.title: U.S. opens hotline for tips about cartels, angering Mexico
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Mexico's president has blasted the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration after it set up anonymous tip lines in the country, accusing American officials of "interference" and not doing enough to fight fentanyl and corruption inside their own borders. Mexico filed a formal complaint with the U.S. over the matter on Friday, Reuters reported . President Claudia Sheinbaum, in harsh comments Thursday, read excerpts from a new investigation by The Associated Press revealing how the DEA allowed at least 1.4 million counterfeit fentanyl pills to go unseized as it spent eight months tracking a drug trafficking ring flooding the Southwest with deadly drugs. "The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot," Sheinbaum said, pointing to the AP report. "The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organized crime, or what they call terrorist groups." "It's clearly an act of interference," Sheinbaum added. Imagine, she mused, if Mexico "opened a WhatsApp service for reporting corruption in the United States. How would the U.S. government view that?" Sheinbaum's angry response comes less than 24 hours after DEA Administrator Terry Cole announced the tip lines on his X account, encouraging Mexicans to denounce members of criminal networks in Sinaloa state, the corrupt officials who support them and people who launder money to finance narcoterrorism. "Your information matters. Your identity and your safety matter," Cole said, specifying that tips submitted via Signal, WhatsApp and email would be handled confidentially. U.S. steps up pressure on Mexico The United States has stepped up pressure on Mexico to fight the cartels and has even offered to deploy troops on Mexican soil, something Sheinbaum has ruled out while maintaining that there will be security cooperation with Washington, "but without subordination." On Nov. 20, Mexican military forces captured drug lord Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, alias "El Chapo Isidro," a key ally of a Sinaloa cartel faction. The FBI had placed him on its list of 10 most wanted fugitives , while the U.S. State Department offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest. The military operation o capture him tsparked panic in the region, sending civilians fleeing from erupting gunfire. Elsewhere in the state, suspected gang members reportedly erected improvised roadblocks. In clashes with security forces , 16 cartel suspects were killed, officials said, and four soldiers also died. Mexico requested Washington's support for the operation, and the United States sent a drone to help gather information about the drug lord's whereabouts. The U.S. has requested Meza Flores' extradition, but Mexican Attorney General Ernestina Godoy said he will be tried in Mexico. Chapo Isidro's capture came just days after Sheinbaum met President Trump on the sidelines of a summit in Asia. Mr. Trump, who has pushed Mexico to do more to tackle drug gangs, said Friday that the two had discussed trade and security. The Mexican government has knocked out several cartel kingpins. Chief among them was Mexico's most powerful cartel leader , known as "El Mencho ," who was killed in February. Similar to the capture of Meza Flores, the dramatic operation resulted in a burst of violence and burning cars. Although cooperation between the two countries went smoothly in that operation, tensions arose between Mexico and Washington in late April after federal prosecutors in New York made public a drug trafficking indictment against Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya , a member of Mexico's governing party. He and nine other officials were accused of collaborating with a faction of the Sinaloa cartel, which the Trump administration has designated a foreign terrorist organization. Amid the controversy, Rocha Moya took an indefinite leave of absence, and his bank accounts in Mexico were frozen. But Mexican authorities refused to carry out the U.S. request to arrest him. Former Sinaloa Security Secretary Gerardo Mérida Sánchez surrendered to U.S. authorities in May. DEA accused of "walking" fentanyl DEA whistleblowers in June revealed to the AP how agents in New Mexico in recent years permitted hundreds of thousands of fentanyl pills to go unseized. At the time, the DEA denied it ever knowingly allowed the trafficking of a synthetic opioid the White House has designated a "weapon of mass destruction." That denial, however, was further contradicted by new AP findings that the DEA permitted at least 1.4 million additional pills to be trafficked between August 2024 and April 2025 as it closed in on the largest fentanyl bust in U.S. history. The AP based its tally on thousands of pages of court documents, investigative records, detailed wiretap reports and 12 hours of DEA surveillance footage showing dealers moving large packages of pills in plastic bins and duffel bags that passed through highly transited hotels, apartment complexes, Airbnb rentals and self-storage facilities in six states. The Mexican president in her comments Thursday called the DEA's decision to permit fentanyl to hit the streets the "Fast and Furious of Fentanyl," a reference to the 2011 gun-walking scandal in which straw buyers smuggled some 2,000 assault weapons into Mexico with the intent of tracing the firearms to cartel leaders. "What is the United States doing in the United States?" Sheinbaum asked. "We have a prosecutor's office here, and the Security Ministry works here. So they should pay close attention to the other side of the border." The DEA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Cole said a channel for submitting tips about the state of Jalisco would be made public Thursday. The state is a stronghold of the powerful Jalisco New Generation Cartel, known by its Spanish initials CJNG, which Washington also designated a terrorist organization. Meanwhile, a veteran DEA agent also told CBS News last month the agency has contributed to the problem by allowing fentanyl pills to reach the streets. "For three years, I've told my DEA managers that we're allowing dangerous amounts of fentanyl to hit the street, and we're doing nothing to stop it, and they didn't listen to me," DEA Special Agent David Howell told CBS News in his first television interview. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/us-opens-hotline-tips-cartels-angering-mexico/

item.title: Supreme Court to tackle AR-15 bans in blockbuster 2nd Amendment case
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A gun store employee holds an AR-15 semi-automatic rifle in Salem, Oregon, on March 6, 2025. - Kevin Neri/Statesman Journal/USA Today Network/Reuters Fourteen years after a lone gunman carried out the deadliest elementary school shooting in American history, the Supreme Court is turning to a bitter legal fight over whether communities may outlaw the type of weapon used in that massacre — a popular class of semi-automatic guns that includes the AR-15. In one of the most notable Second Amendment cases to reach the 6-3 conservative court in decades, the justices will hear arguments Wednesday over state and local bans on “assault-style” weapons, such as the AR-15, some of which were enacted or strengthened in response to a dramatic increase in mass shootings since 20 first graders and six educators were killed in 2012 at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut. For the government officials and gun safety groups defending the bans, the memory of deadly shootings involving the AR-15 is a driving force. “The basic function of government is to keep its citizenry safe, and these guns are so incredibly dangerous in a densely populated area like Chicago,” said Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke, a Democrat, who is defending one of the bans at the Supreme Court. “One hundred percent of the children who were hit with this weapon at Sandy Hook died.” But two trends have emerged in recent years that benefit gun rights groups. First, far more Americans own an AR-15 today — as many as 26 million people, according to one estimate — than even a decade ago. The Supreme Court acknowledged as much last year, noting in a unanimous opinion that the weapons are “widely legal,” purchased by “many ordinary consumers” and that the AR–15 “is the most popular rifle in the country.” Second, the court’s conservatives has quickly and vastly expanded the scope and meaning of the Second Amendment. In a series of landmark decisions, the court found for the first time that the Constitution provides individual Americans a right to own a handgun at home and to carry that weapon outside . It has made it easier to bring guns onto private property open to the public, such as stores. It has required governments defending gun laws to find a “historical antecedent,” a similar rule on the books when the Second Amendment was ratified in 1791. In a 2008 decision that gun rights groups will cite heavily during arguments this week, the late conservative Justice Antonin Scalia suggested that the Second Amendment protects weapons that are in “common use.” The plaintiffs challenging the AR-15 bans in Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, use the phrase “common use” 56 times in their main brief supporting their position. Twenty-seven wooden angel figures stand in a wooded area beside a road, in Newtown, Connecticut, on December 16, 2012, following the mass shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School. - Lisa Wiltse/Corbis/Getty Images The Trump administration, which is backing the gun rights groups, used that phrase 49 times in its own brief filed in September. Kostas Moros, director of legal research and education at the Second Amendment Foundation, acknowledged that AR-15s are dangerous. But he noted that all firearms are dangerous — and, despite that, the framers protected Americans’ ability to own them in the Constitution. “They gave the people the uninfringeable right to keep and bear arms, and that is a right of the people — not of the states, not of the government — to decide,” Moros said. Dangerous and unusual Blockbuster appeals at the Supreme Court are often complicated. The case over AR-15 bans, by contrast, is relatively straightforward. Connecticut and Cook County are leaning into the Supreme Court’s reasoning in a 2022 precedent, New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen , which struck down a strict requirement in New York that residents show cause to obtain a carry permit. As part of that decision, a 6-3 majority concluded that in order to survive a Second Amendment challenge, modern-day gun regulations needed to have some grounding in the “nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.” While the court has tinkered with that standard in subsequent decisions, the state and county say there is an extensive history — dating to medieval times — of English laws banning especially dangerous weapons. Their briefs spend considerable ink discussing bans on crossbows and certain lances. “From fourteenth-century England to twenty-first century America, governments have restricted weapons because of their unusually dangerous properties,” Connecticut officials told the Supreme Court this fall. “In each instance, legislatures have determined that a weapon is atypically lethal relative to its peers — and so have acted to prevent that weapon’s use.” Thomas, who wrote the majority opinion in Bruen, seemed to dismiss the relevance of some of that same history when it came to handguns, noting that one of those laws came “more than 200 years before the birth of Shakespeare, more than 350 years before the Salem Witch Trials.” But he flicked at the idea that banning “launcegays” may have made sense given that they were carried when “one intended to engage in lawful combat.” Supporters of the ban see that logic as a potential opening. Connecticut and Cook County — which includes Chicago — note the AR-15’s ties to its military counterpart, the M16. They note that AR-15s, like other long guns, are more accurate than handguns. The weapons, which first came onto the commercial market in the 1960s, can feature a bullet that tumbles on its axis when it hits a target, creating more significant wounds, the state and county said. The weapon’s design limits recoil more than many hunting rifles, allowing a shooter to maintain control even during rapid, semi-automatic firing. Burke, the Cook County prosecutor, said the weapon’s range and design make it “unbelievably dangerous for law enforcement.” “It was designed for the military,” she said. “It was designed to take out enemy combatants at the greatest distance possible.” A bullet impact crater is seen in concrete, after a gunman opened fire with an AR-15 at the Edmund Burke School in Washington, DC, on on April 28, 2022. - Ricky Carioti/The Washington Post/Getty Images Gun rights groups focus first on the weapon’s popularity. Only 11 states have approved bans on AR-15s, and so the rifles are widely available and in use by gun owners across the country, the vast majority of whom never commit a crime. The plaintiffs challenging the bans described the AR-15 as the “paradigmatic American rifle” in written arguments. According to one survey, roughly 30% of American gun owners have an AR-15 or similar rifle, which works out to 26 million people. A Washington Post-Ipsos survey from 2022 works out to about 16 million Americans. Those numbers alone, the plaintiffs said, should resolve the case in their favor. Scalia’s 2008 precedent in District of Columbia v. Heller “stands for the proposition that arms in common use cannot be banned,” the plaintiffs told the justices. The challengers also reject the idea that an AR-15 is more dangerous than other guns. They argue that the caliber most often used is smaller than that of many traditional hunting rifles. And they scoff at some of the warnings from government officials as bordering on science fiction. “These are ordinary rifles,” the plaintiffs told the justices in one brief, “not phasers from Star Trek.” “If a madman was going to my daughter’s school, I wouldn’t feel much better if he quote-unquote only had a Glock, versus an AR-15,” said Moros, whose group is one of the plaintiffs challenging the bans. “My theory has always been, you need to make targets less vulnerable to attack, rather than worry so much about what the particular gun does.” Counting to five Connecticut and Cook County face headwinds for another reason: At least four conservative justices have signaled skepticism with the bans to varying degrees. If that holds, it means the government will need to find at least two justices to reach a five-vote majority, assuming the court’s three-justice liberal wing supports them. Justice Clarence Thomas, among the court’s most stalwart conservatives, made clear in 2015 that he felt lower courts upholding the bans were “relegating the Second Amendment to a second-class right.” A year later, in a case involving stun guns, Justice Samuel Alito wrote that “the relative dangerousness of a weapon is irrelevant when the weapon belongs to a class of arms commonly used for lawful purposes.” Justice Neil Gorsuch has been less clear, though he voted last year to hear a similar case dealing with Maryland’s AR-15 ban. Associate Supreme Court Justices Samuel Alito, Jr., Clarence Thomas and Brett Kavanaugh attend President Donald Trump's second inauguration, in the Rotunda of the US Capitol on January 20, 2025. - Chip Somodevilla/Pool/AFP/Getty Images Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a conservative who is closer to the center than Alito or Thomas, wrote in the Maryland case that the state was “something of an outlier” by having a ban on the weapons. And, he said, given that millions of Americans own one, the challengers had a “strong argument” that AR-15s are protected by the Second Amendment. As an appeals court judge in 2011, Kavanaugh also dissented from a decision upholding a Washington, DC, ban on “assault-style” rifles. If that holds, it means there will be an enormous amount of focus on Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Amy Coney Barrett at the arguments Wednesday. Still, groups that support additional gun regulations say they’re optimistic about the appeal. The earlier cases dealt with handguns, they note, which are more commonly used for home defense. And most federal appeals courts to review the laws — including the 7th Circuit in the Cook County case and the 2nd Circuit in the Connecticut dispute — upheld the laws. “The chief and Justice Barrett have articulated a history-based test that looks for something useful in the history. It doesn’t just look for a Constitution frozen in time. It looks for a way in which the Constitution can still have relevance,” said Billy Clark, associate litigation director at the Giffords Law Center. The chief justice, Clark said, is “someone who recognizes the consequences” of the court’s decisions, and “I think is going to be cautious about saying that these sorts of weapons are constitutionally enshrined.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/27/politics/supreme-court-ar-15-ban-second-amendment
Matched: law(+3), court(+2), who(+2)

item.title: CIA reportedly did more post-9/11 waterboarding than previously acknowledged
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Satellite image of a facility known as Salt Pit near Kabul, Afghanistan, taken on 17 July 2003. Photograph: REUTERS Newly released documents suggest that the CIA waterboarded more detainees during the post-9/11 “war on terror” than previously acknowledged, utilizing a site north of Kabul, Afghanistan, for the practice of simulated drowning. The agency has acknowledged waterboarding three men: Abu Zubaydah, believed to be a high-ranking member of al-Qaida; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, suspected architect of the 11 September 2001 attacks; and Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, accused of planning the 2000 bombing of a navy destroyer. But declassified documents obtained under a freedom of information lawsuit by the New York Times , includes an account from a former CIA contract translator that appears to support the belief that waterboarding was more common and may have occurred beyond two acknowledged “special rendition” sites in Thailand and Poland. The outlet reported on Friday that the linguist worked at a secret prison, or black site, one north of Kabul, Afghanistan, known as Salt Pit or Detention Site Cobalt. The translator told an FBI agent in 2012 he had seen a man he called “Bahir” strapped to a board tilted downward into water. “There were approximately three to four people ‘doing this,’” the FBI agent summarized in the account, saying that the witness “saw the incident in passing but did not participate himself. The waterboard session was in the hallway and there was not a lot of room.” The account comes from an investigation into the CIA’s use of torture and its destruction of waterboarding videotapes from 2008 to 2012 conducted by then-special prosecutor John Durham. No charges were ever brought. In the new documents produced by the Times , the linguist told the FBI in that “Bahir” was “a relative of Hekmatyar”, seemingly a reference to Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, the former Afghan prime minister. That may correspond to a man named “Ghairat Bahir”, who was apprehended in a raid in Islamabad in 2002, appears in CIA records, and was subjected to “enhanced” interrogation techniques. This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/newly-released-documents-suggest-cia-152503666.html

item.title: Nvidia Blackwell chips turn up at China site tied to alleged spy Alice Huang
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Bloomberg) -- A pair of Chinese firms installed Nvidia Corp.’s powerful Blackwell semiconductors in a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, the woman at the heart of a controversy surrounding the US chipmaker. Most Read from Bloomberg SAP Weighs Cutting at Least 10,000 Roles in AI Restructure Trump Calls GDP Numbers ‘Fake,’ Demands Probe After Revision South Africa Sentences Russia Army Recruit as Ukraine Urges Action Nvidia Rehires Huang in Stunning Reversal After Trump Push Billions in Data Center Deals Grind to Halt After Chip Curbs The gear installed at the Yangtze River Delta Project included a GB300 NVL72 rack, among Nvidia’s most powerful products, according to a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November. Shanghai Shuoyao offered the hardware as collateral to obtain a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank, according to filings from the lender that were reviewed by Bloomberg News. A second firm Shanghai Kezhan, controlled by a Tokyo-based parent, described a GB200 server — which also relies on Blackwell chips — at the facility. That description was provided in documents when it obtained a 90 million yuan loan in late 2025 from a finance-leasing firm wholly owned by a local Shanghai government agency. The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia’s Blackwell processors found their way into a Chinese data center that has ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. These processors were until recently Nvidia’s most powerful data center products, and they’ve always been illegal to ship to China without a US license. President Donald Trump has explicitly said he doesn’t want these chips — which OpenAI and Anthropic PBC use to train their most cutting-edge models — going to the Asian country, at least for now. Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, meanwhile, once claimed they were too big to smuggle: a standard two-meter-tall GB300 NVL72 server rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, can weigh more than 1,500 kilograms (3,300 pounds) and is about the size of a gigantic fridge. Nvidia and its just-reinstated CEO have come under intense scrutiny in recent weeks for their failure to stop diversion of the company’s products to China, a shadow trade that US officials believe is worth billions of dollars. It’s unclear how the GB300 rack made its way to the country, to Shanghai Shuoyao or to this specific site — described in local media as designed to house as many as 800,000 servers. By inputting the serial number for the product into a public warranty database, Bloomberg found that it was manufactured by Taiwan’s Gigabyte Technology Co., which assembles Nvidia chips into servers and racks. The database also provided a model name for the serial number, which matches a GB300 NVL72 server rack manufactured by the Taiwanese company. This sort of gear often passes through several hands — including local distribution networks — before it’s installed in data centers. In many cases, products that were ultimately smuggled into China were originally sold to parties in unrestricted areas. Bloomberg provided the rack’s serial number to Gigabyte, seeking information about to whom Gigabyte had originally sold the hardware and when. It declined to answer those questions, citing company policy. The firm “conducts all business in compliance with applicable laws and regulations,” a spokesperson said in an emailed statement. “All transactions are subject to our internal compliance requirements and the relevant laws and regulations in effect at the time.” Shanghai Shuoyao — the company that procured the GB300 rack and offered it as collateral — is active at the data center linked to Alice Huang and also has significant overlap with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is under US investigation over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia chips to China, Bloomberg has reported. Shanghai Shuoyao, which hasn’t responded to Bloomberg queries over the past year, confirmed this month in a rare public statement that it is one of Megaspeed’s service providers, describing the partnership as “limited to ordinary commercial cooperation.” Megaspeed, meanwhile, used a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project in 2024 to describe its largest data center to investors, dubbing the site a “specific area” facility in an unnamed country. Bloomberg does not have evidence that Megaspeed itself diverted Nvidia hardware there, and Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing in response to the US probe. The company has not answered repeated queries about the Yangtze River Delta Project. Nor has Nvidia, which for years insisted that there was no black market for its products and didn’t respond to questions for this story. The Trump administration this month put Megaspeed on a US trade blacklist, citing a significant risk of involvement in chip diversion. Alice Huang in 2023 founded Megaspeed, a so-called neocloud that won a coveted stamp of approval from Nvidia within four days of its creation, and went on to become the chipmaker’s largest Southeast Asian customer. She also has ties to a number of companies that invested in the Yangtze River Delta Project, which counts Kang Wei as its president. Kang has been introduced at times as Alice Huang’s romantic partner, people familiar with the matter said. It’s unclear how far along operators are in meeting their overall goal for that project, which at 800,000 servers would be on par with hyperscale facilities used by companies like OpenAI. It’s also unclear what mix of servers they plan to use. The parameters they’ve outlined in construction plans reviewed by Bloomberg — specifically, the total processing power as compared to the energy input — would be extremely difficult to satisfy with chips from Chinese companies such as Huawei Technologies Co. Still, the smuggled hardware disclosed in the filings reviewed by Bloomberg is just a fraction of what they’d need. These documents only cover hardware offered as collateral for loans — providing a small snapshot of the operators’ ambitions, while also underscoring how some Chinese financial institutions, including with government ties, were aware that restricted hardware was getting into China and willing to lend capital on those assets. Bloomberg was unable to reach the leasing company that lent money to Shanghai Kezhan, nor Shanghai Innovation Bank, which in addition to the money it lent Shanghai Shuoyao, also provided a 200 million yuan loan to another company called Shanghai Longjie, similarly with restricted Nvidia chips as collateral. Shanghai Longjie — which has the same parent company as Shanghai Shuoyao — disclosed in documents filed to regulators that it has servers containing Nvidia’s earlier Hopper-generation chips, which are illegal to ship to China without Washington’s permission, Bloomberg reported this month. That hardware was manufactured by Super Micro Computer Inc. and Dell Technologies Inc. It’s unclear whether the shipments had US approval. Those aren’t the only Hopper chips at the Yangtze River Delta Project. Shanghai Kezhan, the company that described the GB200 server in filings last year, also disclosed that it has 32 servers with H200 chips there. These products had a Gigabyte prefix in their model name, but the documents didn’t include serial numbers — making them harder to trace. Shanghai Kezhan is headquartered about half a kilometer from the Yangtze River Delta Project, at the same commercial complex where Shanghai Shuoyao solicited engineers to work on Nvidia H100 and H200 chips — two restricted models. In February 2024, both of these firms added “imports and exports” to their business activities, according to data from Qizhidao, a company information provider. The same month, Megaspeed’s original parent — the Chinese gaming giant 7Road — obtained 16.7% of Shanghai Kezhan via a subsidiary the gaming company bought from Alice Huang in 2019. The other 83.3% of Kezhan is ultimately owned by NeXPower Japan, according to Qizhidao. Japan’s official companies registry returned only one company named NeXPower, which was established in March 2025. Caixin, a Chinese business news outlet, said the Tokyo firm is controlled by Alice Huang. Bloomberg has been unable to reach NeXPower for comment. Chinese-speaking staffers at the firm’s registered address wouldn’t confirm that was NeXPower’s office, and shut the door after Bloomberg News asked about their relationship with Alice Huang and Shanghai Kezhan. On the intercom was a message saying they are working and will not respond to media questions. The registered address of the company’s director appeared to be a vacated residence. In May 2025, records compiled by Big Trade Data show, Shanghai Kezhan received a shipment worth $11 million, flown from Malaysia to Shanghai Pudong International Airport with the company as consignee. The customs document described the shipment as “storage chassis,” referring to a structure that houses components of a storage server. But the product code it was assigned to was 847150, which denotes computing servers. The shipment’s unit price was $264,108, too costly for a storage chassis — but within the price range of servers powered by Nvidia’s Hopper chips. --With assistance from Mari Kiyohara, Natsuko Katsuki and Mayumi Negishi. item.title: Hackers breach U.S. Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Mike Stone and Raphael Satter WASHINGTON, Nov 27 (Reuters) - Hackers have breached the US Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters, in a development that could jeopardize a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data. The intrusion ‌at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so during work to upgrade the system, two of the people said, adding that ‌the discovery has led to disruption across the platform. Reuters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the full scope of the intrusion or whether any data had been stolen. In a statement ​to Reuters, the Air Force said it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities." A ONE-STOP SHOP Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve as a one-stop shop for the Air Force's IT needs, combining the resources of four operators — Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet — to power scores of applications including ones that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance. Among ‌them are the Air Force's Cloud-Based Command and Control, which ⁠collates air defense radar and other data feeds from across North America, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 US Air Force locations around the world. SAIC was the prime contractor for Cloud One ⁠until 2025, when Leidos took over. SAIC did not respond to a request seeking comment. Leidos referred questions to the Air Force. Cloud One is among the US military's biggest cloud platforms, according to two of the sources. "A breach here is a big deal," one of the sources said. Investigators have called in Cyber Command, the US military's cyber force, to assess the ​damage, ​one of the sources said. Cyber Command did not respond to requests for comment. A RANGE OF ​DISRUPTION The discovery of the hack led to a range of disruption. ‌Two of the sources, along with a fourth person familiar with the matter, said that efforts to migrate back-office applications to Cloud One, a longstanding military priority, have been paused. Updates to applications already running on Cloud One were blocked, leaving Air Force personnel unable to apply fixes just as a new batch of serious software vulnerabilities has been disclosed across the technology industry. A fifth source said that some users had their administrator rights revoked. All five sources spoke on condition of anonymity. One source said that the cyber intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the control plane. That person likened the control plane to a universal remote, as intruders ‌in theory could leverage their access to check the operational status of military aircraft or the ​movement of spare parts, though it was unclear whether the hackers did so in this case. Reuters ​could not identify the specific vulnerability exploited by the hackers. STRING OF HACKS News ​of the breach comes amid heightened anxiety over AI-powered intrusions, a particularly serious problem for cloud-based networks because of the ability ‌of AI models to swiftly detect weaknesses across wide surface areas. The ​US government already has been dealing with ​the fallout from at least six other recently disclosed cyber incidents, including two at the FBI, a previous hack of Pentagon data, a recent leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel information, a breach affecting at least two spy agencies and a hack at the Treasury Department. Cloud One has long ​been in the crosshairs of hackers. In a 2023 commentary carried ‌by the online publication FedScoop, Cloud One's leadership touted what they called a "100% success rate" in beating back what they said was a "staggering" ​number of attempts to penetrate the platform. "There is no room for error when it comes to security," Cloud One's leadership wrote. (Reporting by ​Mike Stone and Raphael Satter in Washington; Editing by Chris Sanders and Will Dunham) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/exclusive-hackers-breach-us-air-110252874.html

item.title: Netflix drops schizophrenia scene from Tyson Fury doc after wife retracts claim
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Tyson Fury does not have schizophrenia and a scene in which his wife claims he does has been edited out of the Netflix movie about the British boxing superstar. The doc, titled Tyson Fury, provides a tell-all account of Fury’s mental health struggles as he builds up to his fight with Anthony Joshua next month, which is also on Netflix. More from Deadline Netflix Tunes Into Music-Driven Chinese Fantasy Series 'The Melody Of Love' Netflix Posts Racy Thanksgiving Message On 'The Hunting Wives' Season 2 Premiere Day 'Steps' Director Alyce Tzue On "Punk Rock" Inspirations For 'Cinderella' Reimagining The trailer initially showed Fury’s wife Paris Fury saying the boxer is a “mild schizophrenic,” but amid questions from the boxing regulator, this has now been revealed to be untrue. “I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary,” a statement from Paris Fury said. “I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson’s condition and I used the word ‘schizophrenic.’ While Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn’t have this condition and has never received a diagnosis.” A Netflix spokeswoman said the scene has been removed from the doc, which dropped today. “Following new information shared by the family relating to Tyson’s official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch,” she added. Following the schizophrenia comments, which were also included in a Netflix press release about the doc on Monday, the British Boxing Board of Control said it had been examining whether what was thought to be Fury’s diagnosis would get in the way of his long-anticipated fight with fellow British boxer Joshua. That fight has now been cleared to take place on December 11 in Cardiff and could prove to be one of Netflix’s most lucrative live sporting events. Fury’s doc is billed as a “raw, real, unfiltered” look at “the man behind the boxing icon.” Fury has also appeared in two seasons of Netflix’s ob-doc At Home With the Furys, with a third in motion. Both the feature doc and TV show are produced by Banijay-backed Optomen.
